text: Three women, three periods, one day apiece, and the cutting treats them as though they shared a room. The risk in that design is obvious: a structure clever enough to admire and too neat to feel. What keeps that from happening is the scale of what the film chooses to dramatize, which is breakfast, flowers, a cake, a sentence someone cannot finish. Stephen Daldry has 114 minutes for three lives, and the compression pushes almost everything onto faces. Academy recognition went to the lead performance, and that register, interior and held and nearer stillness than display, governs the whole cast. The Hours is less curious about why these women are unhappy than about the hour-by-hour arithmetic of staying, leaving, cooking, writing. Its subject is the weight an ordinary morning can be asked to carry.

At a provincial Catholic boarding school under German occupation, the ordinary business of boys continues: rankings, rivalries, contraband, the small cruelties of dormitory life. Louis Malle took the story from his own childhood, and it shows in what the film declines to underline. It keeps its voice down. War enters as interruption and rumor, as adults with reasons they will not explain, while the camera stays at the height of two boys deciding whether they like each other. The Golden Lion, the César Award for Best Film, and an Academy Award for original screenplay all attached themselves to it, an odd set of prizes for a film so committed to what goes unsaid. Across 105 minutes the tension is carried by classroom routine, and the drama is a matter of what a child understands and how late.

A bargain: she will help him reach the wife who left, and in exchange he owes her something he has not yet agreed to. He has been in an institution and does not pretend otherwise, and the film keeps the negotiations at that level, conducted in a currency of symptoms and favors. David O. Russell keeps it inside a Philadelphia house loud with football, a father's superstitions, and a mother trying to lower the volume. The comedy is real, and so is the risk that illness gets sanded down into charm; the film's answer is to let the arguments run well past the point of comfort. 122 minutes, much of it people standing too close and talking over each other. Most of what it won was for the acting, which is where the pressure sits, since everything depends on whether the two of them are believable when they are wrong.

Two sisters with opinions and a modest income take up with an industrialist's family, and a clerk who has neither is pulled along behind them. This is Edwardian England with the next century already audible, and Margaret Schlegel's liberalism is the test case: easy to hold while the cost stays theoretical, harder when it means marrying into money and being asked to speak for it. James Ivory takes 142 minutes and spends them on rooms, thresholds, and who is permitted to sit down. Its Oscars went to acting, photography, and clothes, and the last two are more central than that ordering suggests, since the argument gets carried by furniture and light as much as by speech. What stands to be lost is not property but the belief that decency survives the crossing of a class line.

Loretta Castorini is thirty-seven, widowed, and has concluded that love is what ruined her luck, so she accepts a proposal from a man she does not love. Then the fiancé's younger brother appears, still furious about the hand he blames his brother for, and the sensible arrangement stops being sensible. Norman Jewison plays it as farce with grief underneath, and the household supplies the machinery: several generations, one kitchen table, everyone's secret half-visible. The dialogue is written to be delivered at volume. The Academy gave it picture, direction, and lead performance; a Silver Bear for direction sits alongside. 102 minutes, and no scene is allowed to idle. What holds it together is that nobody is treated as a joke, including the people behaving ridiculously.

A thriller in which the principal action is two men making telephone calls. All the President's Men opened in 1976, four years after the election it investigates and well after the outcome had become public record, which left Alan J. Pakula a structural problem: the audience already knows. His answer was process. Doors that will not open, a name misheard, a source who confirms nothing and corrects much, 138 minutes of paperwork paced like pursuit. Picture, direction, and editing were the Academy's choices, and the editing is the one to watch, since nearly all the tension is a question of when a cut arrives. The film trusts that watching someone verify a fact twice is worth the time it takes, and it turns out to be right about that.

They meet by accident on a Sunday evening at the school where both their children board, and the drive back is most of the film. Claude Lelouch makes Un homme et une femme out of small talk, weather, a car, and a camera that circles rather than settles; the effect is of overhearing two adults being careful. Whatever they have in common is disclosed slowly and never announced. The exposure here is not the romance so much as the composure each has built to get this far. The Palme d'Or and an Academy Award for international feature sit in its record, a great deal of honor for 102 minutes in which almost nothing is decided out loud. Attention goes instead to hands on a steering wheel and the length of a pause.

Sabotage as a working procedure: loosened bolts, switched signals, a locomotive put where no locomotive should be. La Bataille du rail was made in France in 1946, near enough to the occupation that its derailments were recent practice rather than history, and René Clément films them with flat documentary attention, all depots and timetables and men in overalls, the occupier reduced to an obstacle in the schedule. Its heroes are a stationmaster and his deputy, which sets the scale: resistance conducted by men with clipboards and keys. 85 minutes long, and it holds the Palme d'Or and a prize for direction. Camargue and Athos risk their lives inside an ordinary shift, and the film keeps them there, at the level of the shift.

The soldiers whose survival this film wants are German; the film itself is American, made in 1930. It arrives at the beginning of the sound era, and Lewis Milestone turns the new noise against the material: recruitment speeches first, delivered in classrooms and on parade grounds, then the front takes the volume over. The recruits arrive believing what they were told. The method is attrition, 133 minutes in which the war does not develop so much as continue while the distance between schoolroom rhetoric and the ground keeps widening. Its Academy awards were for picture, direction, and photography. The stake is set out early: a generation was issued a vocabulary about glory, and the front is where that vocabulary gets checked.

195 minutes, and a good share of it is two writers arguing about work. Reds follows the American journalist John Reed through the years he spent reporting a revolution in Russia and trying to import its principles into American labor politics, with Louise Bryant beside him and frequently against him. Warren Beatty directs and plays him, which makes the central vanity part of the subject: a man who cannot separate his convictions from his need to stand at the center of them. The scale is enormous, crowds and congresses and borders, yet the sharpest scenes are domestic, two people negotiating whose work matters this month. The awards came to the two lead performances and to the photography. That a three-and-a-quarter-hour American film about a socialist got made at all is part of the interest.

The author at the center insults nearly everyone he meets, and the film's wager is that 139 minutes in his company can be made bearable. It manages by declining to reform him on schedule. A waitress raising a child alone and an artist recovering from a robbery are the two people who end up in his orbit, and neither is arranged as a lesson for him; both have their own arithmetic of rent, hours, and who can be relied on. James L. Brooks writes the comedy at the level of the sentence, which is why the cruelty stays funny rather than curdling. Both leads were honored, and the pairing is the point, since the thing only works if her patience and his self-regard are performed with equal exactness. The romance is the least interesting element in it.

The swap happens in the first minutes: two Englishwomen in Florence have rooms facing nothing, two other guests offer to trade, and the offer is received as an impertinence. Manners are the whole engine here. James Ivory lets Tuscany do what Tuscany does to a chaperoned young woman with a fixed itinerary, then returns her to England, where the itinerary is waiting. The film is comic about propriety and entirely serious about what propriety costs, and the costs are counted in small refusals rather than scenes. Cinematography, costume, and direction took the Academy prizes, which suits a film in which a hat, a hedge, and a view are load-bearing. 117 minutes, and the most consequential events look, from outside, like nothing at all.

More than thirty years in prison, handed to a young man caught smuggling drugs, less as punishment than as a demonstration. Midnight Express takes that sentence as its premise and then shrinks to what can be seen from inside, where the appeals of a lawyer, a family, and a government arrive as hearsay and the guards' routine is the only reliable clock. Alan Parker directs for physical effect, heat and corridors and the sound of a door, and the 121 minutes are built to be endured rather than followed. Honors went to direction, editing, and score, which are exactly the instruments of that pressure. Innocence was never the question here; time is, and the film is built to make its passage physically felt, hour by hour and shift by shift.

The two of them make a pact that neither will ask the other to change. Ben has come to Las Vegas to drink himself to death and says so without drama; Sera has her own reasons for accepting terms like those, and what follows comes from the agreement being kept. Mike Figgis holds the city to small rooms and afternoon light instead of spectacle, and the 111 minutes stay close to two faces. The production is French, the material about as American as material gets. It would be easy to play this as squalor or as rescue; the film takes neither, settling for tenderness administered under conditions that do not allow for it. The awards it took were for the two performances, and they are earned in negative space, since neither character is granted the speech that would explain them. What they give each other is company.
